baseline.title: Alice, Bob, and the Windy Mitten
baseline.text:
Alice had a best friend who was a cat, and his name was Bob. Bob was orange as a marmalade tart, with white socks on his back feet and a tail that curled like a question mark.

One windy Saturday, they walked to the park together. Alice wore her red woolly mittens, the ones Grandma had knitted, with a lumpy pom-pom on each thumb. Bob trotted beside her, his little bell going ting, ting, ting.

At the swings, Alice pulled off one mitten to tie her shoelace. Then a gust of wind went WHOOSH, and the mitten went flying. It tumbled over the grass and disappeared.

"Oh, no," said Alice. She looked under the slide. She looked behind the bench. "Grandma will be sad if I lose it."

Bob sat down in the middle of the path. He lifted his nose, twitched his whiskers, and sniffed the air. Sniff, sniff, snuffle. Then he set off at a trot, with his tail held high like a flag.

"Wait for me!" called Alice. She hurried past the sandpit and past a family of ducks who quacked at them crossly. Bob led her all the way to the big oak tree beside the pond.

There he stopped. He pawed at a tangle of roots. Something red poked out from underneath, flapping gently, like a tired little bird.

Alice knelt down and peeked into the roots. Inside was a tiny nest. Three speckled eggs sat in it, and snuggled right beside them was Alice's red mitten. A brown sparrow popped up from the edge, cheeping in a worried way.

"Oh," whispered Alice. "You've made a cozy bed for your babies."

She stayed very still, so she would not scare anyone. Bob sat still too, with his tail wrapped around his paws.

"I want my mitten back," Alice said softly. "But your eggs need it to stay warm. What should we do?"

Alice thought hard. She looked at the mitten, then at the nest, then at her bare hand. Her fingers tingled in the chilly wind.

Then she had an idea. She reached into her coat pocket and pulled out the crust of toast she had saved for the ducks. She crumbled it on the grass, far away from the roots.

"That's for you, Mrs. Sparrow," she said. "Thank you for keeping my mitten warm."

Mrs. Sparrow hopped down, looked at the crumbs, and looked at Alice. Then she began to peck, peck, peck.

"You can keep the mitten until your babies hatch," Alice told her. "I'll get another one."

Alice walked home with one bare hand. Bob pressed his warm, furry side against her leg the whole way, and his bell went ting, ting, ting, just a little bit slower than before.

When Grandma heard the story, she laughed until her glasses slipped down her nose. "Then we'll knit a new mitten," she said, "with a little brown bird on the thumb."

That night, the wind outside sighed softly. Alice tucked her new mittens under her pillow. Bob curled up at the end of her bed, purring like a sleepy kettle.

Far away, under a big oak tree, a sparrow was dreaming warm dreams.

Goodnight, Alice. Goodnight, Bob.

first_draft.title: Alice, Bob and the Moon's Silver Blanket
first_draft.text:
Alice counted the lanterns the way other children counted sheep. One in the kitchen window. Two in the baker's attic. Three, four, five, six glowing in the village windows, and then she stopped, because something was out of place. On the top of the wooden garden fence, a corner of silver fluttered like a ribbon caught on a nail. It was not a ribbon. It was the moon's blanket, and it had slipped right off.

Bob, her ginger cat, was perched on a fence post washing one paw. "Don't worry, Alice," he said, flicking his tail. "I always know the way. The moon lives at the top of the old oak tree, and we shall carry the blanket home together."

"Are you sure?" asked Alice.

"Absolutely certain," said Bob, and he hopped down with a soft thump.

The blanket was floppy and cool, like pond mist that had been folded too many times. They lifted it between them, and it tickled Bob's nose. "Ah... ah... ACHOO!" A puff of silver dust drifted up into the air. Bob shook himself and marched off toward the pond. "This way!"

They squelched through the reeds. Frogs went plip, plop, plip. Crickets went chirr, chirr, chirr. Then Alice saw a lantern glowing in Mrs. Hobb's window. "We've passed that lantern before," she said.

"Nonsense," said Bob. "That's a different lantern."

They wandered on. The blanket dragged. Bob's ears drooped. Soon they came around the reeds again, and there was the very same lantern, winking at them.

"That's three times," said Alice, and her voice came out grumpy. "You never listen."

"And you never stop counting!" huffed Bob.

Bob flopped down on the damp grass with a plop. Alice's cheeks went hot. She wanted to say something sharp, but instead she sat down beside him and let the blanket puddle into her lap. For a while they just listened to the frogs.

Then Alice looked at the pond. The moon's reflection floated on the water, round and pale, but a bite was missing from one edge, right where the blanket should have been. "Bob," she whispered, "look."

Bob peered over the edge. His whiskers twitched. "Hmm. That's a very odd moon."

"It's missing a corner," said Alice. "The blanket came off the fence, so the hook must be on the oak. I'll count the fence posts back to the tree. One, two, three..."

Bob followed her steps, tail high, careful to put each paw where hers had been. Eleven fence posts later, the old oak loomed over them, its branches creaking softly like an old rocking chair.

Bob went up first, quick as a spark. Alice climbed behind him, counting each branch under her hands. Four branches, five, six. At the very top, a small silver hook gleamed in the leaves.

"Together," said Bob, and for once he didn't sound certain of anything at all. "On three?"

"On three," said Alice. "One, two, three!"

They lifted the blanket up, up, and hooked it over the moon's edge. It settled with a soft sigh, and the whole sky seemed to brighten, as if someone had wiped a window clean.

The moon glowed bright and white. Silver light spread over the rooftops and the sleeping pond. Alice and Bob climbed down the oak and walked home along the fence, side by side, while the lanterns went out one by one.

The friends strolled over the cool grass, their steps growing slow. Bob purred softly, a sound like a kettle far away. Alice counted the lanterns down to one, and then to none. The pond whispered under its blanket of silver light.

They curled up together in the quiet garden, and the village settled into sleep. Goodnight, moon.

baseline.title: Rocket and the Upside-Down Map
baseline.text:
Leo found the map tucked under his pillow after lunch, folded into a tiny square. It was yellow at the edges and smelled faintly of salt, like a faraway sea. A wobbly X sat beside a drawing of a palm tree, and along the bottom were curly words: Follow the sunflowers. Beware the squeaky gate.

"Rocket! We have a real treasure map!" Leo shouted. His golden dog leapt off the rug and thumped his tail so hard that the lamp wobbled. Rocket sniffed the paper, sneezed twice, and wagged even harder. Leo tied a red scarf around his head like a proper pirate. "Aye, aye, First Mate!"

Out in the backyard, the sunflowers stood taller than Leo's head. Their big yellow faces seemed to turn and follow him across the grass. Leo counted them out loud, one, two, three, all the way to nine. Then they tiptoed to the fence, where a paper tag hung from the gate. Eek, went the gate. Eek, eek, eek. Leo tugged at the tag, but the string was knotted high on the top rail, far above his reach.

He tried his best. He climbed onto the wooden bucket, but it wobbled like a jelly. He tried hopping, and Rocket hopped too, barking, "Ruff! Ruff!" Then both of them flopped into the clover in a heap. Leo sat up, rubbed his elbow, and frowned at the knot. Pirates never gave up on a tricky knot, he thought. Maybe they just found a longer stick.

From the kitchen window, Dad called, "Careful with the rake, Captain!" Leo fetched the long garden rake from the shed. Rocket sat on the bucket to hold it steady, his tail sweeping the grass. Leo hooked the rake over the top rail, wiggled it, and pulled. The knot slipped loose, and the tag fluttered into his hand. Rocket barked in delight.

The tag read: Dig where the apple tree shades the X. They marched to the apple tree and dug with a little trowel. Leo found three worms, one smooth pebble, and a sock nobody had missed in weeks. Rocket dug too, flinging dirt over both of them like a snowstorm. Leo's arms ached. He flopped back and stared at the map. Then he turned it all the way around. Oh! The map had been upside down the whole time. The X was not under the apple tree at all. It was beside the shed, right next to the blue wheelbarrow.

"Rocket, we've been digging in the wrong place!" Leo laughed. They raced across the lawn. Rocket's nose found the spot first, and his paws scratched and scrabbled. Thunk! Leo pulled out a little tin box with a rusty latch. Inside sat a pile of chocolate coins wrapped in gold foil, a folded pirate hat, and a dog bandana with skull stickers. A note said, For the bravest crew in the backyard.

Leo put the hat on, and Rocket wore the bandana with great dignity. They carried the tin inside, where Dad gave them a clap and a big hug. Later, Leo tucked the map under his pillow again, next to a single gold coin. He yawned a wide, sleepy yawn.

The room was quiet now. The moon made a silver square on the rug. Rocket curled up at the foot of the bed with a happy sigh, and the house settled around them, soft and slow. Leo closed his eyes. The coin stayed warm in his hand.

"Goodnight, Captain," whispered Dad. "Goodnight, Rocket."

He walked to the mossy stone and knelt down. Rocket pushed past him, nose to the ground, and his tail stopped wagging. He sniffed once, twice, then gave a happy little bark.

After supper, Leo set the seed tin on the windowsill, right beside the folded map. Rocket curled up at the foot of his bed with a long, contented sigh.

The house grew quiet. Outside, the crickets hummed in the grass. Leo pulled up his blanket and looked out at the dark garden.

'Goodnight, garden,' he whispered.

baseline.title: Ember and the Wind Song
baseline.text:
Ember was a little dragon with speckled green wings and a tail that curled like a question mark.

She lived in a cave on top of Mossy Hill, where the air smelled of rain and warm stones.

Every morning, her big brother Brax zoomed past her window. Whoosh! Whoosh! "Come fly with me, Ember!"

Ember tucked her wings tight against her sides. Her tummy went flip-flop, flip-flop.

"Not today," she said softly. "My wings are scared."

Brax laughed a puffy little laugh and zoomed off over the trees.

Ember sighed and climbed to the edge of the hill. She looked down.

The valley looked very far away. The river looked like a thin silver ribbon.

"I'm too little," she whispered. "I'll wobble. I'll flop. I'll land in the pond with a splash."

So she tried. First she flapped her wings very fast. Flap, flap, flap! She didn't lift off. She just blew a breeze that tickled the daisies.

Next she tried a running jump. Thump, thump, thump! She stopped at the edge and tumbled into a bush. Rustle, rustle, scratch!

"Ouch," said Ember, pulling a thistle out of her nose.

She tried hopping on one foot. She tried flapping while standing very still. Nothing worked. Her wings only wobbled, like wet laundry on a windy day.

Ember plopped down on a warm rock and hung her head.

A small brown wren hopped onto the rock beside her. Her feathers were the color of toffee.

"Why the frown?" asked the wren.

"I want to fly," said Ember. "But my wings feel wobbly, and my tummy feels flippy."

The wren cocked her head. "My name is Tilly. Watch me."

Tilly hopped to the very edge of the rock. She spread her wings wide and let herself drop.

Whoosh! The wind caught her. Up she went, up and up, then around in a loop, singing, "Tweedle-dee, tweedle-dee!"

Ember's eyes grew big. "Oh!"

"Your wings know more than you think," Tilly sang, landing beside her. "Wide and slow. Let the wind do the holding."

Ember stood up. She took a deep breath. She smelled rain and pine and warm stone.

"Wings out wide," she whispered. "Wind, come near."

Tilly clapped her wings. "Wings out wide, wind come near! Hold on gently, have no fear!"

Ember giggled. Then she counted softly. "One. Two. Three."

She hopped.

Her feet left the rock. The wind tickled her belly. Her wings wobbled, wibble-wobble, and then, very quietly, they stopped wobbling.

Whoosh! Ember glided over the daisies. She glided over the thistles. She glided over the silver ribbon of the river.

"Whee!" she shouted. "I'm flying!"

Brax zoomed back around the hill. His eyes went round as plums. "Ember! You're flying!"

Ember swooped in a slow, wide circle. Her tummy did not flip. It only giggled.

She drifted down, down, down, and landed in a patch of soft green moss. Bounce, bounce, bounce. Then she sat very still and grinned.

Brax and Tilly landed beside her. "Do it again!" they chirped.

"Tomorrow," said Ember, yawning. "Maybe tomorrow."

They flew home together, the three of them, while the sky turned soft and pink. Ember's wings felt warm and tired.

She curled into her cave, where the moss smelled sweet and the rain tapped gently on the stones.

Tilly tucked her head under one wing. Brax yawned a small, sleepy yawn.

Ember's wings folded slowly, like a blanket.

The wind hummed a little song outside. Hush, hush, hush.

Goodnight, little wings.

Mab stretched and yawned. 'Ember could try,' she said. 'You have wings.'

Mab padded over and curled up by the roots. 'Once there was a cat who flew into a teapot,' she began.

'Was it hot?' asked Ember.

'Very hot,' said Mab. 'So hot that she turned into toast with jam.'

Ember giggled, and a little puff of light floated out of her belly.

She carefully hooked her claws around the string. Tick, tick, went the knot as it came loose. The blue kite wiggled, then floated free.

Ember glided gently down with the kite bobbing above her head. Old Tobin laughed and clapped his dusty hands. 'Well done, little dragon!' He pulled a fresh ribbon of string from his pocket and tied it to the kite.

Then they all walked home together through the golden evening. Mab sneezed at another puff of fluff. Ahhh-choo! Ember laughed so hard that her belly flickered.

The village lights blinked on, one by one. The wind softened to a whisper. Ember's glow faded to a soft ember color. She curled up in the grass beside the blue kite, and Mab purred at her side.

The oak leaves hushed. The stars came out, one, two, three. Ember's hum grew slower and softer. Hmmm... hmmm... hmmm.

Hush now, little dragon. Goodnight.

baseline.text:
At midnight, when the whole house was snoring softly, Mia heard a noise from the kitchen. Tick-a-tick! Boing-boing! Tiddle-diddle-doo!

She tiptoed downstairs in her woolly socks, holding Bear by one floppy ear. The kitchen was silver with moonlight, and a white glow spilled from the fridge like a sleepy sunrise. Mia peeked around the doorway, and her mouth fell open.

Red peppers swayed like lanterns. A row of green beans wiggled on the bottom shelf. Mr. Cauliflower wore a paper crown folded from a napkin, and a leek stood on the counter, puffing on a tiny silver whistle.

"Welcome, welcome!" cried Captain Carrot, hopping onto the milk carton. "Tonight is the Great Crunch Ball! But we have a crumbly problem. The Golden Whistle slid off the counter, and now it is hiding somewhere under the butter dish."

Mia crept closer. She could hear a tiny clink, clink, clink, like a spoon tapping a teacup. Sure enough, a shiny gold glint winked in the dark gap behind the butter dish.

"Oh, my orange knees!" wailed Captain Carrot. "Nobody can reach it. We are too short, too squishy, and too wobbly!"

Mr. Cauliflower flopped forward and bounced off a loaf of bread. Boff! A cucumber rolled right into the butter dish, which wobbled, which wiggled, and which made the whistle slide even further away. Glink!

"Oops," said the cucumber, looking very sorry.

Mia tapped her chin. She could not reach the whistle with her arm, and it was much too far for a leek to puff it out. Then she had an idea.

"Green beans," she whispered, "could you stretch?"

The beans looked at each other. They wiggled. They wobbled. Then, one after another, they stretched long and thin, like a bendy green ladder, until the last bean reached right up to the edge of the counter.

At that moment, a door creaked upstairs. Dad padded into the kitchen in his fluffy dressing gown, rubbing his eyes. "What's all this racket?" he yawned. Then he saw the vegetables, and his eyebrows climbed right up to his hair.

"We're having a party," Mia explained, "and our whistle is lost."

Dad smiled. He lifted the butter dish very carefully, and held it high. "Careful, now," he said.

Mia took a wooden spoon from the drawer. She nudged the whistle, once, twice, and gently, until it rolled out from its hiding place and onto a folded tea towel. Plink!

"Hooray!" shouted Captain Carrot. He lifted the whistle with his leafy hands and blew. PEEEP!

After a while, the music grew slower. The peppers drooped like tired lanterns. The beans curled up into little green bundles. Captain Carrot yawned so wide that his leaves rustled.

"Time for bed, party friends," whispered Mia.

One by one, the vegetables settled back into the cool, quiet fridge. The white glow dimmed to a soft, gentle light. Mr. Cauliflower tucked his crown under his stalks. The whistle was set down on the shelf, right where it could rest.

Dad gave Mia a sleepy hug. Bear was yawning too.

Upstairs, the blankets were warm and the pillow was soft. Mia closed her eyes and listened to the house breathing slowly in the dark.

From the kitchen, very faintly, came one last small sound.

Peep.

Hush now. Goodnight.

first_draft.title: Crispin and the Midnight Fridge Party
first_draft.text:
At midnight, the fridge door creaked open with a long, squeaky "eeeeeek." A silver stripe of moonlight spilled across the kitchen floor. Crispin, a tiny, twitchy carrot in a wobbly bottle-cap crown, poked his orange nose out from behind the butter dish. Inside the fridge, vegetables were hanging paper streamers and stacking cups of cold cucumber.

"A party!" squeaked Crispin, and then he clapped both hands over his mouth. Bubbly sprout punch fizzed in a bowl. The fridge began to hum, hmmmmm, hmmmmm, and the hum turned into a bouncy beat: boom-a-chicka, boom-a-chicka. Crispin's secret was already bubbling up like the punch. He twirled across the checkered tablecloth to find his best friend.

Pea-Pea was bouncing on top of the sugar bowl. Boing! Boing! Boing! "Pea-Pea, there's a secret midnight party in the fridge!" Crispin whispered, which was really more of a squeak.

"Shh!" said Pea-Pea, and he giggled so hard he bounced right off the sugar bowl. Boing!

"We need to check the guest list," said Crispin. They hopped, bumped and rolled to the crisper drawer. There, tucked in his corner with his leaves folded tight, sat Old Thornton, the grumpiest turnip in the whole kitchen.

"Parties are silly," he grumbled. "Noisy, sticky, silly. Nobody invites me anyway."

"But you're not on the list!" Crispin blurted. "Party in the fridge! Midnight! Bubbles and streamers!"

Clink! Clatter! Clink! Down in the spoon drawer, something rattled. A sleepy spoon yawned, "Who's making all that racket?" Crispin clapped his hands over his mouth again, but it was far too late.

"We have to sneak a secret invitation past the spoons," whispered Pea-Pea. "Before they wake up the whole kitchen!"

Pea-Pea went first. He tied a rolled-up note to a sprout and gave it a big push. The sprout bounced, Pea-Pea rolled off the counter, boing, boing, boing, and landed with a soft flop on the tablecloth. "Ta-da!" he giggled. Meanwhile, the note floated down into the fridge and stuck in the cold drip. Plink. Plonk. Soggy and stuck.

Crispin tapped his crown and thought hard. He could not keep a secret, but he could keep a riddle! He scratched words onto the flat top of a bottle cap with his tiny carrot tip. "Purple hat and grumpy frown, sitting in the crisper, upside down? The party's full and the bubbles fizz. Who is missing? Look and see!" Crispin tiptoed to the crisper and gave the cap a tiny tap, tap, tap, under Old Thornton's leaf. Pea-Pea hummed a quiet, sleepy tune, hmm-hmm-hum, to keep the spoons dreaming.

Old Thornton squinted at the bottle cap. "Hmph," he grumbled. "Silly riddle." He read it again. He read it a third time. Then his leaves gave a funny little wiggle. "Well," he mumbled, "I suppose I would love to come. Do they have hats? A turnip needs a hat for a party."

The vegetables cheered a hushed whoop! Whoo-hoo! In the spoon drawer, the sleepy spoons clapped, clap, clap, clap, while the fridge hummed along. Pea-Pea bounced in a wobbly dance, Old Thornton wobbled too, and everyone giggled until their leaves shook.

Crispin lifted his bottle-cap crown and gently placed it on Thornton's head. "Just for a moment," he said proudly. Thornton peered down at it. "Hmph. Very silly," he said, but he wore a wide, sheepish grin.

Soon the music slowed, and the party began to wind down. The vegetables tiptoed back onto the shelves. Crispin, Pea-Pea and Thornton settled into a cozy corner of the checkered tablecloth. The fridge door swung shut with a soft click. The moonlight dimmed to a pale silver glow, and the fridge hummed its gentle lullaby, hmmmm, hmmmm, until the kitchen grew quiet.

"Goodnight, kitchen," whispered Crispin.

"Goodnight, Thornton," whispered Pea-Pea.

Old Thornton gave a tiny snore, and the bottle-cap crown slipped softly down over his leaves.

baseline.title: Wren and the Missing Biscuit
baseline.text:
The house smelled of warm toast and rain, and the hallway light was already turned down low. Wren stood beside her bed in her striped pyjamas and frowned at her pillow. Biscuit was not there.

Biscuit was a floppy grey rabbit with one ear that stood up tall and one ear that never quite made up its mind. He went everywhere with Wren. He came to the bath and to breakfast. Now he was gone.

"Dad!" Wren called down the stairs. "Biscuit is missing!"

Her dad came up two steps at a time, with a tea towel over one shoulder. He looked at the empty pillow, then at Wren's worried face, and he rubbed his chin the way he did when he was thinking hard.

"Right," he said. "Let's be detectives. Where did you last see him?"

Wren closed her eyes and thought. "On the window seat. I was reading him the story about the owl who couldn't whistle."

They looked on the window seat. They found a cushion, a library book about owls, and one red sock that had been missing since Tuesday. They did not find Biscuit.

"Hmm," said Dad. "Detectives always check the places nobody expects."

They tiptoed along the landing. Marmalade, the fat ginger cat who lived with them, was sitting outside the airing cupboard. Her tail was curled around her paws, and her eyes were half closed. She looked very pleased with herself.

"Mrrrp," said Marmalade.

"Marmalade," Wren said slowly, "do you know where Biscuit is?"

Marmalade blinked once, slowly, and said nothing at all. Wren thought that was very suspicious.

Dad opened the cupboard door. A puff of warm air rolled out, smelling of clean sheets and lavender. Towels were stacked high, like sleepy grey hills. Dad lifted the top one. Nothing. He lifted the next one. Still nothing.

Then Wren saw it: the very tip of a floppy ear, poking out from the bottom of the pile. The ear twitched.

"Biscuit!" Wren whispered.

She pulled out the bottom towel very carefully, the way you would lift a sleeping kitten. There, curled up on the softest, warmest towel of all, was Biscuit. His nose was tucked under one paw, and he was making a tiny whistling sound, like a kettle that had only just started thinking about boiling.

"You gave me a fright," Wren told him. Her voice wobbled between being cross and being happy, and she could not decide which one was winning.

Marmalade padded in and rubbed against Wren's legs, purring like a boat engine.

"You kept him warm, didn't you?" Wren said quietly. Marmalade gave a long, satisfied yawn, which was answer enough.

Wren scooped up Biscuit. He smelled of lavender and dust and cat, and his one tall ear flopped down happily against her cheek. Dad laughed softly. "Looks like the case is solved," he said. "Bed, detective."

Back in her room, Dad pulled the blankets up to her chin. Wren tucked Biscuit under her arm, the way he liked best. Marmalade jumped up at the bottom of the bed, turned around three times, and settled down with a sigh.

"Night, Wren," said Dad. He switched off the big light and left on the little lamp shaped like a moon.

The rain tapped gently on the window. The house creaked softly, the way houses do when they are getting ready for sleep. Biscuit's whistle grew slower and softer, like a kettle left to cool.

Wren's eyes felt heavy. Her arm was warm. Her breathing slowed.

Goodnight, Biscuit, she whispered. Goodnight, Marmalade.

Then, very quietly, the house was still.

first_draft.title: Biscuit and the Foggy Lamp
first_draft.text:
Biscuit the ginger cat liked the warm spot beside the kitchen stove best of all. Her fur was as fluffy as a dandelion clock, and it puffed up even more when she stretched.

Old Mabel hummed a sea shanty while she set a dish of peppermints on the table. Her cardigan pocket clinked every time she moved. Biscuit's whiskers twitched. A thin, salty mist was creeping through the crack in the window, and it tickled her nose.

"Ah-choo!" sneezed Biscuit, so hard that her tail shot straight up.

"Bless you, my fluffy bundle," said Mabel, tucking a peppermint into her pocket. Then she stopped humming. Both of them looked up at the wall. The great beam that always swept across it, round and golden, had gone weak and yellow, like a candle at the end of its wick.

"Oh dear," said Mabel. "The lamp has gone dim."

Mabel tucked her polishing cloth into her apron and began to climb the spiral staircase. Clank, clank, clank went her boots on the iron steps. Biscuit padded up behind her, one careful step at a time, her tail held high. The stairs curled round and round like the inside of a seashell.

At the top, the lamp room was full of fog. It was soft and grey and smelled of seaweed. Mabel reached up with her cloth, but the glass was high and the mist was thick, and she could only wipe a small round patch.

Biscuit leapt at the fog and batted at it with both paws. Her paws came away damp, and she sneezed again. "Ah-choo! Ah-choo!"

Just then, pitter-patter, pitter-patter, a small round shape waddled through the open door. It was Puffin Pim, puffed up with importance and very eager to help.

"Pim!" said Mabel. "Just in time, my friend."

Pim wanted to help more than anything. He snatched the polishing cloth in his orange beak. Then the cloth stuck. It stuck fast, flapping from the end of his beak like a flag in the wind. Pim spun in a wobbly circle, around and around the lamp, going "Mmmf! Mmmf!" while the cloth flapped behind him like a tail.

Mabel laughed so hard that her peppermints rattled.

Biscuit stopped batting. She sat very still and watched. The mist did not drift evenly. It rolled out from a gap under the window frame, where a little draught whistled in. The grey curls gathered there, thick as wool, and crept over the corner of the glass. That was where the light could not get out.

Biscuit trotted over, took the loose end of the cloth gently in her teeth, and tugged. Pim let go with a surprised "Mmph!" The cloth dropped to the floor. Biscuit hopped onto the windowsill, pushed the cloth up with her nose, and rubbed the fogged corner back and forth. Squeak, squeak, went the glass. A patch of gold appeared, then another, and then the whole corner shone.

The lamp blazed out bright and golden. Its beam swept across the cove and lit up the water all the way to the rocks. Far away, a small fishing boat with a red sail came gliding safely in.

"Hooray!" said Pim, with the cloth still stuck to his beak.

Down in the kitchen, Mabel and Pim shared one peppermint at the table. Biscuit curled up on the rug beside the stove, where it was warm and smelled of toast and salt.

The kitchen grew quiet and soft. The kettle ticked as it cooled. Outside, the lighthouse beam swept slowly over the sleepy water, round and round, like a gentle hand patting the waves. Biscuit tucked her nose under her tail and curled into a ginger ball.

Mabel began to hum one last low shanty. The room grew dim, and then still.

Hush now. Goodnight, Biscuit.

baseline.title: The Goose Who Honked at Midnight
baseline.text:
Once upon a farm, a goose named Gertrude had a very loud honk. HONK! It rattled the windows. It shook the hay. It woke up every animal in the barn.

One night, Gertrude could not find her hat. It was a tiny yellow hat with a red feather. She loved that hat more than anything.

"Where is it?" she honked. "Where is it? HONK, HONK!"

Her friend Pig snored in the straw. Snore, snort, snore. "Maybe it is under the hay," he mumbled, and went back to sleep.

Cow looked behind the water trough. Moo, moo, splash! Nothing but a frog. The frog croaked, "Ribbit! Not here!"

Gertrude felt a wobble in her tummy. She took a deep breath. Then she heard a soft little sound. Tap, tap, tap.

It was coming from the top of the hay pile. There sat Owl, blinking her big round eyes. On her head was something small and yellow.

"Oh!" said Owl. "I found this hat floating down from the rafters. I thought it looked lonely."

Gertrude laughed so hard she hiccupped. HIC! Then she honked, "HONK! Thank you!"

Owl gave a sleepy wink. "Tomorrow, let's play a quieter game."

Pig yawned. Cow yawned. The frog yawned too, with a tiny ribbit.

Gertrude tucked her hat under her wing. Her honk grew softer. Hoo... hon... hush.

The barn grew still. The straw grew warm. Snore, snort, snore. Shh, goodnight, little farm.

first_draft.text:
Bartholomew the tortoise lay under his big leafy oak, eyes shut tight, his shell warm in the sun. "Nap time," he grumbled. "Peace and quiet. That's all I want."

Thump! Pip the duckling tumbled over the mossy stone wall, head over webbed feet. "Hee hee! Hic!" she giggled. "I'm hiding! Don't look!"

Crash! Mo the puppy bounded in right behind her. His tail wagged so hard that his whole body wiggled. Wiggle, wag, wiggle, wag! His tail swept Bartholomew's teacup right off its rock. Clink! "I'm counting!" Mo barked. "One, two, three... ten!" He covered his eyes with one floppy paw and peeked through the other.

Then came more. Bunnies bounced. Hedgehogs rolled. Kittens pounced, and a little lamb trotted in with a bleat. "Ready or not, here we come!" they shouted.

Bartholomew sighed. "Shoo! Shoo! Go away!" But the animals only giggled louder. They hid in his flowerpots. They squeezed behind his rocks. Pip crawled under his blanket and hiccupped so hard that the blanket hopped up and down. "Hic! Hic! Hic!" The whole meadow giggled along.

Bartholomew tried shooing once more, and the game only got louder. He stopped. He took a long, slow breath. Then, very softly, he hummed the low, sleepy tune he used to hum on warm afternoons. Hmmmmm. Hmmmmm.

The giggling slowed. The bunnies stopped bouncing. The kittens stopped pouncing. One by one, yawns spread through the crowd. "Would you like to rest?" Bartholomew asked. "There's a big heap of soft leaves right here."

Pip waddled over and flopped into the leaves. Mo padded after her, and his tail swished slower... slower... until it stopped. Pip gave one last tiny hiccup. Then she was quiet.

Soon the whole crowd was piled in the leaves, warm and still, as the moon rose over the glowing silver pond.

The animals curled up, their breathing slow and soft. The pond whispered. The oak leaves rustled. Silver moonlight spilled over the mossy wall. Bartholomew tucked his head into his shell and let out a happy little sigh. "Goodnight, little friends," he whispered.

baseline.title: The Monster Under Puddle Bridge
baseline.text:
Under the old stone bridge on Puddle Lane lived a monster named Grumbleguts. Everyone in Pebble Town knew he was there, because his tummy rumbled louder than thunder.

"I eat people!" he bellowed one windy evening, so loudly that the bridge shivered and the ducks flapped off in a fright. "Every single one of you! Gobble, gobble, CRUNCH!"

Ada Finch, who was seven and a half and not easily scared, stepped up to the railing with a flashlight in one hand and a jar of honey in the other. Her grandma had tucked it into her coat pocket that morning.

"Which people do you eat?" Ada asked.

Grumbleguts blinked his three big eyes. Nobody had ever asked him that before. "Well," he mumbled, "people who are late for bed, mostly."

"Oh," said Ada. "Then you should know I'm very late. It's nearly dark."

Grumbleguts looked up at the sky, then at the moon, and his tummy gave a sad little gurgle. "I've been hungry for three whole days," he said. "Every time I come out, everybody runs away squealing. Monsters can't chase supper. We get too tired."

Ada sat down on the cold stone step. She tapped the honey jar with one finger. Tap, tap, tap. "I think you need a picnic," she said. "Nobody can run away from a picnic."

"But I don't have any food," Grumbleguts said.

"Yes you do," said Ada. "You have me, and my friends, and a whole street full of kitchens."

Ada ran up her front steps, where the porch light glowed warm and yellow. Her mom and dad listened with their eyebrows up. Then her dad grinned and said, "Well, let's see what's in the pantry."

Soon Milo had his red wagon, and June had a basket of apples still dusty from the orchard. Mrs. Pim sent a crusty loaf of bread. The baker's girl knocked with oat cookies wrapped in paper. Mr. Okoro offered a block of cheese that smelled like sunny afternoons.

They pulled the wagon down the lane, its wheels squeaking like tiny mice, and spread a blanket beside the bridge. Grumbleguts's ears wiggled.

He took a bite of bread. Crunch. He took a bite of apple. Crunch, crunch. He took a honey-dipped cookie, then another, then one more, humming with every mouthful. "Gobble," he said softly. "Gobble, gobble, mmm."

"Is he gobbling people?" Milo whispered.

"No," giggled June. "He's gobbling cheese."

Then Grumbleguts gave a tiny hiccup, HIC, and a puff of crumbs flew out of his mouth. Everyone laughed until their tummies hurt, even Grumbleguts, whose laugh sounded like a bathtub being emptied.

He was not hungry anymore. He yawned, a yawn so big that a moth flew straight into it, and he patted his round belly. "I'm sorry I shouted," he said. "I didn't know anyone would share."

"Next time, knock first," said Ada, "and bring a cookie."

Her dad called from the lane, so the children folded the blanket and stacked the empty wagon. Grumbleguts waved one huge, floppy hand as they walked home, and the bridge did not shiver once.

Back in bed, Ada listened. Under the bridge, a soft, happy rumble drifted up the lane, like a sleepy cat purring. The moon slid behind a cloud. The wind hushed. Far away, a duck gave one small quack and tucked its head under its wing.

Goodnight, Puddle Lane. Goodnight, Grumbleguts. Sleep now, all of you.

first_draft.title: Grumble and the Moonlit Cookie
first_draft.text:
At dusk, just as the lamps blinked on along Pebble Lane, Grumble's tummy began to rumble. RUMBLE-grr-BOOM! It sounded like thunder rolling over a faraway hill. Grumble was a shaggy monster, as round and soft as a haystack, with feet as big as washtubs.

"Cookie dinner," he rumbled, waddling to the bakery with the striped awning. Mabel was yawning behind the counter, a smudge of flour on the tip of her nose.

"Your cookie is cooling on the windowsill," she said. "I'll fetch you some milk."

Grumble leaned toward the sill, where one warm golden cookie sat. The window was open a crack. A gust of wind whooshed through the room, and the cookie went tumbling out the door like a runaway wheel. Only a lonely crumb was left behind.

"Oh, no, no, no," groaned Grumble. He hurried outside just in time to see his cookie bounce across the lane and roll up the grassy hill, glowing under the silver moon.

On the hillside, Grumble peered up at the sky. "It looks just like a cookie," he whispered. "A very big, very silver cookie!"

He stacked a tower of wobbly rocks. Wobble, wobble, CLONK! The rocks tumbled down. Next he grabbed a bedsheet from a clothesline and flapped it like a net. Whoosh! Flump! The sheet landed on his head, and he stumbled about, bonking into a tree.

Then he tiptoed toward a dandelion puff, fluffy as a cloud. He sniffed it. Ah-CHOO! Seeds whirled everywhere. Ah-choo! Ah-CHOOO! "Moon, you are too tricky," he sniffled.

A tiny crumb trail led down a sloping hole under a bush. Grumble followed it, bumping along a burrow tunnel, until he popped out into a cozy room. There sat two fluffy rabbit sisters, Pip and Poppy, sniffing his cookie with twitching noses.

"Our tummies are very hungry," said Pip.

"Very, very hungry," said Poppy.

Grumble's tummy gave a grumble. He looked at the cookie. He looked at the rabbits. Then he broke the cookie into three crumbly pieces, gave the biggest share to Pip and Poppy, and kept the smallest for himself. He licked his paws, gave a small shrug, and smiled a wide, crumbly smile.

Soon a bobbing lantern came up the hill. It was Mabel, with a basket of fresh cookies on her arm and a yawn on her face. She stopped, looked at the rabbits, and let out a laugh that echoed across the hillside.

Just then Grumble's tummy rumbled again. RUMBLE-grr-BOOM!

final.title: Grumble and the Moonlit Cookie
final.text:
At dusk, just as the lamps blinked on along Pebble Lane, Grumble's tummy began to rumble. RUMBLE-grr-BOOM! It sounded like thunder rolling over a faraway hill. Grumble was a shaggy monster, as round and soft as a haystack, with feet as big as washtubs and fur that smelled of rain and clover.

"Cookie dinner," he rumbled, waddling to the bakery with the striped awning. Mabel was yawning behind the counter, a smudge of flour on the tip of her nose, and the whole room smelled of butter and honey.

"Your cookie is cooling on the windowsill," she said. "I'll fetch you some milk."

Grumble leaned toward the sill, where one warm golden cookie sat, its edges crinkled like a smile. The window was open a crack. A gust of wind whooshed through the room, and the cookie went tumbling out the door like a runaway wheel. Bumpity, bumpity, bump! Only a lonely crumb was left behind.

"Oh, no, no, no," groaned Grumble. He hurried outside just in time to see his cookie bounce across the lane and roll up the grassy hill, glowing under the silver moon.

On the hillside, Grumble peered up at the sky. "It looks just like a cookie," he whispered. "A very big, very silver cookie! But how do I get a bite?"

He stacked a tower of wobbly rocks, one on top of another, tall as his knee. Wobble, wobble, CLONK! The rocks tumbled down and rolled into a puddle. Next he grabbed a bedsheet from a clothesline and flapped it like a net. Whoosh! Flump! The sheet landed on his head, and he stumbled about, bonking into a tree. Boink!

Then he tiptoed toward a dandelion puff, fluffy as a cloud. He sniffed it. Ah-CHOO! Seeds whirled everywhere, dancing in the moonlight. Ah-choo! Ah-CHOOO! "Moon, you are too tricky," he sniffled, rubbing his nose with one enormous paw.

A tiny crumb trail led down a sloping hole under a bush. Grumble followed it, bumping along a burrow tunnel that smelled of earth and sleepy roots, until he popped out into a cozy room lit by glowworms. There sat two fluffy rabbit sisters, Pip and Poppy, sniffing his cookie with twitching noses.

"Our tummies are very hungry," said Pip.

"Very, very hungry," said Poppy.

Grumble's tummy gave a small, sad grumble. He looked at the cookie. He looked at the rabbits. Then he broke the cookie into three crumbly pieces, gave the biggest share to Pip and Poppy, and kept the smallest for himself. He licked his paws, gave a small shrug, and smiled a wide, crumbly smile.

Soon a bobbing lantern came up the hill, swinging side to side. It was Mabel, with a basket of fresh cookies on her arm and a yawn on her face. She stopped, looked at the rabbits and the monster with crumbs on his chin, and let out a laugh that echoed across the hillside.

Just then Grumble's tummy rumbled again. RUMBLE-grr-BOOM!

"I think you need another cookie," said Mabel.

They all went back down to the bakery steps and shared the warm batch. Grumble's tail wagged slowly, back and forth, thump, thump, against the step. Pip and Poppy giggled, and crumbs tumbled off their whiskers.

Grumble, Mabel and the rabbits sat together, quiet and full, as the moon floated higher. Crickets hummed softly in the grass. The bakery window glowed gold. Grumble's tummy finally stopped rumbling as he curled up in the warm grass, sleepy and content.

"Goodnight, Pip. Goodnight, Poppy. Goodnight, moon," he whispered.

baseline.title: The Ghost Who Couldn't Stop Hiccupping
baseline.text:
The house at the end of Crooked Lane had a squeaky gate, a wobbly chimney, and a ghost who could not stop hiccupping.

Nell had moved in with her Gran only a week before, and she heard the ghost every single night. First came the creak of the attic stairs. Then came a long, wobbly moan, like wind through a keyhole. Then came the noise that rattled the windowpanes: HIC! A pause. HOOOO! HIC!

"Nobody can sleep through that," Nell whispered, pulling her quilt up to her nose. Under the bed, Gran's cat, Marmalade, had gone as flat as a pancake, and the lamp on the nightstand flickered every time the hiccups came.

Nell tiptoed downstairs in her socks, holding her flashlight tight. In the parlor, a round, silvery ghost floated above the armchair. He wore a bow tie made of cobweb, and he looked dreadfully embarrassed. "Oh, I am sorry," he said. "I'm meant to be frightening. I practised my moan all afternoon. But every time I get going, out pops a HIC!"

"Maybe you could hold your breath," Nell suggested.

"I haven't any breath to hold," sighed the ghost, and he drifted through the wall and back again.

Nell tried to help in her own way. "BOO!" she shouted.

"HIC!" went the ghost, and every picture on the wall swung sideways.

"That made it worse," said Nell, rubbing her ears.

Gran came down the stairs in her fluffy blue dressing gown, carrying a mug of warm milk. "When I had hiccups," she said, "I sipped from the far side of the cup."

The ghost tried, but the mug slid straight through his fingers and clattered onto the rug. Gran's eyebrows rose. "Well. That was a fine try."

Nell sat down on the rug and watched him closely. Each hiccup came right after a big, gulping breath, the kind people take when they have been startled. "What if you breathe slowly?" she said. "Like you're blowing out birthday candles, only there's no cake."

The ghost puffed out his cheeks. He let the air go in a long, thin whistle. "Whooooo." Then he tried again, slower. In through his nose, out through his mouth. Each breath came softer than the last. HIC became hic, and hic became a squeak no louder than a mouse in a teacup.

"Again," Nell whispered, and she breathed along with him. In, two, three. Out, two, three. The parlor grew as still as a snowy field, and the clock on the wall ticked slower and slower.

At last the ghost gave one very small hoo. He smiled a wobbly smile and sank into the rocking chair, which creaked gently. "Thank you, Nell," he said. "Tomorrow I'll manage a proper moan. A quiet one."

Upstairs, Marmalade crept out from under the bed and curled up at the foot of Nell's blanket. The house settled with a sigh, the way a house does when it is ready for sleep. Nell's eyes grew heavy. The last thing she heard was the rocking chair, creak, creak, creak, going slower and slower, until it stopped altogether.

Goodnight, Bartholomew. Goodnight, Gran. Goodnight, Marmalade. Goodnight, house.

first_draft.title: Mr. Wobble and the Lantern in the Basket
first_draft.text:
The old house on Larkspur Lane had a habit of talking after dark. Its stairs groaned. Its floorboards sighed. So when Ethan heard a soft, wobbly whisper drifting down the hallway, he only pulled his blanket up to his nose and reached for his flashlight.

"It's just a draft," he told himself. But drafts do not whisper, "Oh dear, oh dear."

Ethan tiptoed past the long row of coats. They swayed on their hooks, and one sleeve brushed his cheek like a cold, floppy hand. He clicked on his flashlight. Behind the coat rack something giggled, a bubbly sound like lemonade fizzing in a glass.

"Who's there?" Ethan whispered.

The coats parted, and out floated a pale ghost with a sheet that rippled like pudding. He had round cheeks, a tall, shaky hat, and knees that knocked together.

"I'm Mr. Wobble," he said, and giggled again. "Sorry. I giggle when I'm nervous. I'm not very good at being scary."

"I wasn't going to scream," said Ethan. "Why are you hiding?"

"My lantern is lost," said Mr. Wobble. "It's the glowing one I carry up the stairs to my attic. Without its light I can't see a single step, and I keep ending up at the bottom again."

Ethan clicked his flashlight twice. "Then let's find it."

They crept to the creaky staircase. Eeeek, went the third step. Ethan pressed down with his toe, and the board wiggled loose. "Loose board," he said. "Not your lantern."

Mr. Wobble giggled so hard he floated straight into the hat stand. Hats tumbled onto his head, one after another. Plop. Plop. Plop.

Next they tiptoed to the window at the top of the hall. Whooo, whistled the wind through a crack. The curtain flapped in and out, flap, flap, flap.

"Ghost or draft?" Ethan asked.

"Draft?" squeaked Mr. Wobble, and he zipped back into the hat stand with a clatter.

Then the closet door gave a long, squeaky creeeak. Mr. Wobble gasped, giggled, and bumped the umbrella stand. Ethan laughed so hard he had to sit down on the bottom stair.

When the laughing settled, the house went quiet. Ethan closed his eyes. He didn't chase the next creak. He just listened.

There, low and warm, like a kettle before it starts to sing, came a soft hum.

"Mr. Wobble," Ethan whispered, "hum again."

The ghost hummed, a little wobbly, and Ethan followed the sound. Past the coats. Past the stairs. All the way down the hallway to the kitchen, where the stove still glowed orange and the air smelled of toast.

In the corner sat a cat basket. Inside it, a round orange cat named Pickle snored like a tiny motorboat. Under the blanket, a faint gold light leaked out around the edges.

"Hum again," Ethan breathed.

Mr. Wobble hummed. Under the blanket, the gold light flickered, like a wink.

Ethan knelt beside the basket. "Pickle," he said softly, "would you like the warm spot by the stove?"

Pickle opened one eye, said, "Mrrp," and went back to snoring. Ethan scooped him up, blanket and all, and tucked him onto the warm tiles beside the stove. Pickle stretched, flopped over, and was asleep again before his tail touched the floor.

Ethan lifted the lantern out of the basket. Its light spilled across the kitchen floor in ripples of gold.

He held it out. "I think this belongs to you."

Mr. Wobble's eyes went round as lamps. He took the lantern with both hands, and it glowed bright gold. The coats in the hall glowed too. Mr. Wobble hummed, floated up the stairs, and every creaky step sang a soft note as he passed.

At the top step he turned and waved. "Goodnight, Ethan," he called, and then he slipped into the attic and was gone.

Ethan tiptoed back down the long hallway and up to his room. He switched off his flashlight and slid under his quilt. The house settled into quiet. The stairs stopped creaking. Far below, Pickle purred on his warm spot by the stove.

At the attic window, the last gold light faded slowly into the night.

"Goodnight, old house," Ethan whispered.

And the house, very softly, hummed back.

final.title: Mr. Wobble and the Lantern in the Basket
final.text:
The old house on Larkspur Lane had a habit of talking after dark. Its stairs groaned. Its floorboards sighed. So when Ethan heard a soft, wobbly whisper drifting down the hallway, he only pulled his blanket up to his nose and reached for his flashlight.

"It's just a draft," he told himself. But drafts do not whisper, "Oh dear, oh dear."

Ethan tiptoed past the long row of coats. They swayed on their hooks, and one sleeve brushed his cheek like a cold, floppy hand. He clicked on his flashlight.

Then the coats went utterly still. Not one sleeve stirred. A cold whisper hung in the air, thin as a thread. Ethan's breath made a little cloud. Then, from behind the coat rack, came a bubbly giggle, like lemonade fizzing in a glass.

"Who's there?" Ethan whispered.

The coats parted, and out floated a pale ghost with a sheet that rippled like pudding. He had round cheeks, a tall, shaky hat, and knees that knocked together.

"I'm Mr. Wobble," he said, and giggled again. "Sorry. I giggle when I'm nervous. I'm not very good at being scary."

"Why are you hiding?" asked Ethan.

"My lantern is lost," said Mr. Wobble. "It's the glowing one I carry up the stairs to my attic. Without its light I can't see a single step, and I keep ending up at the bottom again."

"Then let's find it."

They crept to the creaky staircase. Eeeek, went the third step. Ethan pressed down with his toe, and the board wiggled loose. "Loose board," he said. "Not your lantern."

Mr. Wobble giggled so hard he floated straight into the hat stand. Hats toppled off the rack and bonked onto his head, one after another, each with a hollow plunk.

Next they tiptoed to the window at the top of the hall. Whooo, whistled the wind through a crack. The curtain flapped in and out, flap, flap, flap.

"Ghost or draft?" Ethan asked.

"Draft?" squeaked Mr. Wobble, and he zipped back into the hat stand with a clatter.

Then the closet door gave a long, squeaky creeeak. Mr. Wobble gasped and bumped the umbrella stand. Ethan laughed until he had to sit on the bottom stair.

When the laughing settled, the house went quiet. Ethan closed his eyes. He didn't chase the next creak. He just listened.

There, low and warm, like a kettle before it starts to sing, came a soft hum.

"Mr. Wobble," Ethan whispered, "hum again."

The ghost hummed, a little wobbly, and Ethan followed the sound. Past the coats. All the way down the hallway to the kitchen, where the stove still glowed orange and the air smelled of toast.

In the corner sat a cat basket. Inside it, a round orange cat named Pickle snored like a tiny motorboat. Under the blanket, a faint gold light leaked out around the edges.

"Hum again," Ethan breathed.

Mr. Wobble hummed. Under the blanket, the gold light flickered, like a wink.

Ethan knelt beside the basket. "Pickle," he said softly, "would you like the warm spot by the stove?"

Pickle opened one eye, said, "Mrrp," and went back to snoring. Ethan scooped him up, blanket and all, and tucked him onto the warm tiles beside the stove. Pickle flopped over and was asleep before his tail touched the floor.

Ethan lifted the lantern out of the basket. Its light spilled across the kitchen floor in ripples of gold.

He held it out. "I think this belongs to you."

Mr. Wobble's eyes went round as lamps. He took the lantern with both hands, and it glowed bright gold. The coats in the hall glowed too. Mr. Wobble hummed, floated up the stairs, and every creaky step sang a soft note as he passed.

At the top step he turned and waved. "Goodnight, Ethan," he called, and then he slipped into the attic and was gone.

Ethan tiptoed up to bed. He switched off his flashlight and slid under his quilt. The house settled into quiet, and the stairs stopped creaking. Far below, Pickle purred by the warm stove.

At the attic window, the last gold light faded slowly into the night.

"Goodnight, old house," Ethan whispered.

And the house, very softly, hummed back.

baseline.title: Sir Hob and the Wobbly Duel
baseline.text:
On a windy evening in the village of Thimbleford, Sir Hob the knight stood in the castle yard, swinging his wooden sword at a straw dummy named Bartholomew. Whoosh! Clonk! Plink! The sword flew out of his hand and landed in a puddle with a sad little splash.

"Again!" puffed Sir Hob. His helmet slid down over his nose, and he pushed it back up with a clank.

Nell, his small squire, sat on the mounting block with a bag of toffee apples. "You're trying too hard, Sir Hob," she said, licking her sticky fingers.

Tomorrow was the Harvest Fair, and the sword contest was the most exciting thing in the whole county. The winner would receive a golden pear made of shiny tin. Sir Hob wanted that pear more than anything.

So he tried a heavier sword. It was so heavy that when he swung it, he spun round and round like a wobbly top, until he bumped right into the water trough. SPLOSH! Water dripped from his plume, and Nell giggled so hard she dropped a toffee apple.

Next he tried wearing his long red cloak, to look fierce. The cloak wrapped itself around his ankles, and he tumbled into a haystack. "Oof!" he said, from somewhere deep inside the hay. His elbow was a little sore, so he lay there for a while, looking up at the stars.

A grey mare named Mabel poked her nose over the stable door and snorted, as if to say, Well? Sir Hob sat up and rubbed his elbow. He thought and thought.

"Nell," he said slowly, "what if I stopped trying to look like a knight in a storybook, and just practised being me?"

Nell shrugged. "Then you'd be Sir Hob, who sneezes whenever the hay tickles his nose."

Sir Hob laughed. Then he had an idea. "Let's play tag with swords. You have to keep your feet moving and your sword as loose as a wiggly worm."

So he took off his cloak and hung it on the fence. He hopped left. He hopped right. He held his sword lightly, the way you hold a spoon of warm porridge, and tapped Nell's shield. Tick, tick, tick! Nell tapped back. Tock, tock, tock! Soon they were both giggling so loudly that the hens woke up and grumbled from their roost.

The next morning, the fair was full of bunting, the smell of gingerbread, and the tootling of a little brass band. Sir Gildo the Great, tall and proud, stood at one end of the field. Sir Hob stood at the other, with his cloak folded neatly on Mabel's back.

"Begin!" shouted the judge, Mistress Pimm.

Sir Gildo swished his sword high. Sir Hob's feet danced left, then right. Tick! His sword tapped Gildo's shield. Tock! Gildo tapped back, and his plumed hat wobbled off his head and landed in a bucket of apples.

For a moment, nobody moved. Then Sir Gildo began to laugh, a big booming laugh that echoed across the field, and Sir Hob laughed too.

"Well!" said Mistress Pimm, wiping her eyes. "I have never seen a duel end so happily. You shall both have a golden pear, for the best dancing I have ever seen."

That night, Sir Hob hung his helmet on a peg by the door. Nell curled up in the warm hay with her golden pear tucked under her chin. Mabel snored softly in her stall, and the candle on the windowsill burned low and gold.

Outside, the wind had gone quiet. An owl hooted once, far away, and then the village was still.

Sir Hob pulled up his blanket and yawned, slow and wide.

"Goodnight, Nell," he whispered.

"Goodnight, Sir Hob," said Nell, already half asleep.

The candle flickered, and then it was dark, and everyone was dreaming.

first_draft.title: Sir Pip and the Goose's Crooked Crown
first_draft.text:
On the stone bench beside the fountain, Sir Pip polished his shiny helmet with the corner of his cloak until it gleamed like a spoon. Tomorrow was the castle tournament, and Pip was ready to show everyone how brave a knight he was. The knights would race around the garden in a friendly contest instead of fighting with swords. Pip had practiced all week.

He lifted the helmet, set it on his head, and stood up very tall. Then it slid down with a clonk and covered both of his eyes.

"Oh, bother," said Pip, wobbling in a small circle. "How can a knight race if he cannot see his own boots?"

While he fumbled with the buckle, a shadow fell across the bench. HONK! Gulliver the goose strutted up, his crooked gold crown tipped over one eye. Before Pip could lift his visor, the goose grabbed the blue banner with its golden star and tugged it off the bench.

"Honk! Mine now! Honk-honk-HONK!" Gulliver flapped his wings and waddled away, the banner trailing behind him like a long tail.

High above, the clock tower began to hum. Pip knew what that meant. The bell would ring for bedtime soon, and his banner had to be back before then.

"Give that back!" Pip clanked after the goose, straight into a tall rose hedge. Thump! The leaves smelled sweet, like honey, but his helmet blocked his view, and all he could see was green.

"Oh my, Sir Pip," said a warm voice. Duchess Marigold came down the path with a basket on her arm and a spare ribbon tied at her wrist. She laughed a kind laugh, the sort that made you want to laugh too. "Gulliver has taken many shiny things in his time. Come, I'll show you the stepping-stone path behind the fountain. But a helmet makes a poor pair of eyes, and the banner is yours to find with your own wits."

Pip followed the stones, hopping from one to the next. Plip, plop, plip. Then he stopped. The garden was quiet except for the fountain gurgling and the clock humming. He lifted his visor and listened hard.

HONK, came a sound from the herb corner. Then, softly, another honk.

On the hedge, a loose thread of gold glinted in the last of the sunlight. Pip followed it past the thyme and sage, around a wheelbarrow, and under a low branch. There sat Gulliver on an upturned flowerpot, trying on his crooked crown. Beside him, the blue banner lay crumpled in the mint.

Pip did not rush. He hummed while he thought. "Gulliver," he said politely, "that is a fine crown. Would you like to admire the shiniest helmet in the whole castle? You may look at it as long as you like, if you let me have my banner back."

Gulliver tilted his head. His beady eyes went from the crown to the gleaming helmet and back again. Then he dropped the banner into the mint, waddled over, and gave the helmet a long, proud stare. "Hmm," he honked softly.

Pip picked up the banner, shook out its golden star, and bowed low. "Thank you, Sir Goose."

He tucked the banner under his arm and walked back along the stepping stones with Marigold. Behind them, the clock tower gave a soft ding. Bedtime was coming, and Pip had kept his promise.

Pip and Marigold strolled slowly along the path as the lanterns glowed amber. The fountain murmured, sleepy bees hummed in the roses, and the clock struck its last gentle chime. Pip hung the banner by the window on its wooden hook, yawned a big yawn, and rested his helmet on the bench, where it stayed put while the stars came out over the quiet garden. Goodnight, Sir Pip.

baseline.title: Mira and the Ninety-Six Muffins
baseline.text:
On a rainy Tuesday, Mira sat at the kitchen table with her math worksheet and a stubby pencil. The last question was the trickiest one of all. What is 12 times 8? She chewed the end of her pencil. It tasted like wood and a little like yesterday's pancakes.

"Twelve times eight," she whispered. "Twelve. Eight. Eight-y twelve?" Her cat, Biscuit, hopped onto the table and sat right on top of the worksheet. "Biscuit, you are not a helpful math tutor," said Mira, gently lifting him off. Biscuit blinked and yawned a very large yawn.

Across the room, Nana Ruth was stirring a pot of apple soup. The kitchen smelled of cinnamon and warm bread. "Stuck on something?" Nana asked. Mira nodded. "I keep losing count of all the eights." Nana wiped her hands on her apron. "Then let's count with something you can touch."

Nana took a muffin tin from the cupboard. It had twelve round cups, and they clinked softly when she set it down. "Pretend each cup is a basket for the school bake sale," Nana said. "Each basket holds eight muffins. How many muffins for all twelve baskets?" Mira touched each cup with her finger. One, two, three, all the way to twelve. She tried to picture the muffins, golden and speckled, but the picture kept wobbling like jelly.

So she tried beans. She dropped eight dried beans into the first cup, then eight more into the second. Her fingers grew sticky. A bean rolled under the stove. Biscuit pounced on another with a tiny "rrp!" and skidded across the floor on his socks. Mira giggled. "Biscuit, that is not helping!" But she picked up her pencil again, and the beans kept coming back to her, one by one.

Then Mira stopped and took a slow breath. Eight, sixteen, twenty-four. Counting eights was like climbing a hill with a heavy bag. She looked at the twelve cups and thought about them differently. Twelve was ten and two. Ten baskets of eight made eighty. Two more baskets made sixteen more. "Eighty," she said slowly, "eighty-eight, ninety-six!"

"Ninety-six is a lot of muffins," said Nana, peeking over the top of the soup pot. "How could you check?"

Mira tapped her pencil and tried again from the other side. Eight twelves. Twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six, forty-eight, sixty, seventy-two, eighty-four, ninety-six. She counted on her fingers, all ten of them, and then two more. Both ways made ninety-six. She wrote the number neatly at the bottom of the worksheet, and it sat there, tall and proud, like it had been waiting for her.

The rain tapped softly on the window now, slower than before. Nana turned down the stove. The apple soup sighed and bubbled in a quiet way. Mira set her pencil in its cup and let her shoulders drop. Biscuit climbed into her lap and curled into a warm, round ball.

The kitchen lights dimmed to a honey glow. Mira's eyelids grew heavy, and the numbers on the page began to blur into soft shapes. "Goodnight, muffins," she whispered. "Goodnight, ninety-six."

baseline.title: Maya and the Button Bird
baseline.text:
On Sunday night, Maya sat on the edge of her bed and swung her feet. Tomorrow was Monday. Tomorrow she would start at a new school.

"What if nobody likes me?" she whispered.

Her mom sat down beside her. The bed went creak, creak, creak. "What if they do?" her mom said softly.

Maya thought about that. She pulled a yellow button from her pocket. It was round and shiny, and it had four little holes like tiny windows.

"This was from my old school," she said. "My friend Lila gave it to me."

On Monday morning, the classroom was loud. Chairs scraped. Shoes squeaked. Everyone already had a group. Maya stood by the door with her button in her fist.

She wanted to say hello. The words stuck in her throat like a lump of oatmeal.

Then she heard a sound. Plip-plop. Plip-plop. It came from the corner, where a boy named Teo was drawing a bird on his paper.

The bird had a long tail that curled like a question mark.

"Your bird is fancy," Maya said.

Teo looked up. "It's a button bird," he said. "It needs a button for its nest."

Maya held up her yellow button. Teo's eyes grew as round as cookies.

"Can I borrow your bird?" Maya asked. "I could give it a nest."

So they made a nest together. Teo drew twigs. Maya glued the yellow button in the middle. A girl named Priya came over to see. Then a boy named Oscar came, too. Soon the whole table was full of crayons and giggles.

"Cheep-cheep!" Oscar sang, flapping his arms. Everybody laughed, even Maya.

At lunch, Maya sat near the window. Her heart went thump, thump. But Priya waved. "Come sit with us," she said. So Maya did.

That afternoon, the bird drawing sat on the windowsill, right beside the sunshine. The yellow button caught the light and sparkled.

When the bell rang, Maya walked out with her mom. Her backpack bumped softly on her back.

"How was it?" her mom asked.

Maya grinned. "Noisy. And a little bit wonderful."

That night, Maya sat on the edge of her bed again. She swung her feet slowly. Creak. Creak. Then she was still.

The room grew dim. The hallway light made a soft yellow stripe on the floor. Outside, a owl hooted, low and gentle.

Maya tucked her blanket up to her chin. She closed her eyes.

Hoo, said the owl. Hush, said the wind.

And Maya drifted off to sleep.

Goodnight, Maya.

Goodnight.

first_draft.title: Maya and the Squeaky Welcome
first_draft.text:
Maya stood by the classroom door on her first day at a new school, which was a Monday. Tap, tap, tap went her shoes. They were red and shiny, and they had never tapped so much before.

Inside, a bright room waited for her. A rainbow rug stretched across the floor. A cozy reading corner held squishy pillows, and a big oak tree leaned against the window, as if it wanted to peek in.

"SQUEEEAK!" The sound came from a cage by the window. Maya jumped so hard her backpack bounced. A round brown guinea pig stood up on his back legs and stared right at her.

"That's Biscuit," said Mrs. Lin, the teacher, with a smile. "He squeaks at everyone who is new. It's his way of saying hello."

Biscuit stopped squeaking. He wiggled his nose up and down, up and down, twitchy as a jelly bean. Maya giggled a tiny giggle. For one whole second, her shoes stopped tapping.

During circle time, everyone sat on the rainbow rug. Maya found a spot on a red stripe and folded her hands. Children talked about their pets and their favorite snacks. Maya wanted to say her name, but the words stuck like peanut butter on the roof of her mouth.

When the boy beside her said, "I like dinosaurs!" the circle moved on. Maya's shoes went tap, tap, tap. She stayed quiet.

At lunch, Maya carried her tray into the noisy cafeteria. Trays clattered. Chairs scraped. Every table was full of chatting friends. Maya stood still, holding her tray, with no idea where to sit.

"Tomorrow," she whispered. "I'll try again tomorrow." Her shoes kept tapping.

Then she noticed a girl at the end of a long table. Her backpack sparkled with glittery star stickers. She held her tray in both hands and looked around, just like Maya was doing.

That's Ruby, Maya thought. Ruby was the one who had clapped the loudest on the rug.

Maya took a deep breath. Tap, tap, tap went her shoes. Then she walked over.

"Hi," she said. "There's an empty seat by the window. Do you want to sit with me?"

Ruby's face lit up like a sunny morning. "Really? I don't know where to sit."

"Me neither," Maya said, and she laughed a small laugh. She pulled out her crackers, the square ones with cheese. "Want some?"

Ruby took one and crunched. "These are the best crackers ever!" Then she sat down beside Maya, and her star stickers winked in the light.

After lunch, the class went back to the classroom. Biscuit squeaked when Ruby walked in, and then he wiggled his nose at her.

"He likes me!" Ruby giggled.

"He does," said Maya. "Want to give him a piece of carrot?"

They took turns holding a tiny slice. Biscuit sniffed Maya's fingers, nibbled Ruby's carrot, and wiggled his nose again. Maya's shoes lay still on the rainbow rug, side by side.

When the bell rang at the end of the day, Maya and Ruby waved from the window. Under the big oak tree, Ruby's mom waved back.

"See you tomorrow!" Ruby called.

"See you tomorrow!" Maya called, waving with both hands.

That night, Maya snuggled into her cozy bed. The clock on the wall ticked softly. Tick, tock. Tick, tock. Far away, a faint squeak drifted up from Biscuit's cage, like a goodnight.

Her red shoes rested by the door, quiet at last. Outside, the oak tree's leaves whispered in the breeze. Maya closed her eyes and thought about tomorrow, and about a friend waiting at the lunch table.

Shh. Goodnight, Biscuit. Goodnight, Ruby. Goodnight, Maya.

final.title: Maya and the Squeaky Welcome
final.text:
Maya stood by the classroom door. It was her first day at a new school, and it was Monday. Tap, tap, tap went her shoes. They were red and shiny, and they had never tapped so much before.

Inside, a bright room waited for her. A rainbow rug stretched across the floor. A cozy reading corner held squishy pillows. A big oak tree leaned against the window. It looked like it wanted to peek in.

"SQUEEEAK!" The sound came from a cage by the window. Maya jumped so hard her backpack bounced. A round brown guinea pig stood up on his back legs and stared right at her.

"That's Biscuit," said Mrs. Lin, the teacher, with a smile. "He squeaks at everyone who is new. It's his way of saying hello."

Biscuit stopped squeaking. He wiggled his nose up and down, up and down, twitchy as a jelly bean. Maya giggled a tiny giggle. For one whole second, her shoes stopped tapping.

During circle time, everyone sat on the rainbow rug. Maya found a spot on a red stripe and folded her hands. Children talked about their pets and their favorite snacks. Maya wanted to say her name, but the words stuck like peanut butter on the roof of her mouth.

When the boy beside her said, "I like dinosaurs!" the circle moved on. Maya's shoes went tap, tap, tap. She stayed quiet.

At lunch, Maya carried her tray into the noisy cafeteria. Trays clattered. Chairs scraped. Every table was full of chatting friends. Maya stood still, holding her tray, with no idea where to sit.

"Tomorrow," she whispered. "I'll try again tomorrow." Her shoes kept tapping.

Then she noticed a girl at the end of a long table. Her backpack sparkled with glittery star stickers. She held her tray in both hands and looked around, just like Maya was doing.

That's Ruby, Maya thought. Ruby was the one who had clapped the loudest on the rug.

Maya took a deep breath. Tap, tap, tap went her shoes. Then she walked over.

"Hi," she said. "There's an empty seat by the window. Do you want to sit with me?"

Ruby's face lit up like a sunny morning. "Really? I don't know where to sit."

"Me neither," Maya said, and she laughed a small laugh. She pulled out her crackers, the square ones with cheese. "Want some?"

Ruby took one and crunched. "These are the best crackers ever!" Then she sat down beside Maya, and her star stickers winked in the light.

After lunch, the class went back to the classroom. Biscuit squeaked when Ruby walked in, and then he wiggled his nose at her.

"He likes me!" Ruby giggled.

"He does," said Maya. "Want to give him a piece of carrot?"

They took turns holding a tiny slice. Biscuit sniffed Maya's fingers, nibbled Ruby's carrot, and wiggled his nose again. Maya's shoes lay still on the rainbow rug, side by side.

When the bell rang at the end of the day, Maya and Ruby waved from the window. Under the big oak tree, Ruby's mom waved back.

"See you tomorrow!" Ruby called.

"See you tomorrow!" Maya called, waving with both hands.

That night, Maya snuggled into her cozy bed. The clock on the wall ticked softly. Tick, tock. Tick, tock. Far away, a faint squeak drifted up from Biscuit's cage, like a goodnight.

Her red shoes rested by the door, quiet at last. Outside, the oak tree's leaves whispered in the breeze. Maya closed her eyes and thought about tomorrow, and about a friend waiting at the lunch table.

Shh. Goodnight, Biscuit. Goodnight, Ruby. Goodnight, Maya.

baseline.title: Biscuit's Window Stars
baseline.text:
The house was quiet in a way Sam did not like. Downstairs, the kettle hummed. Outside, an owl called hoo, hoo, hoo. But there was no jingle of Biscuit's tag, no click of toenails on the wooden floor, and no thump, thump of a tail against the bed.

Sam pulled his blanket up to his chin. At the foot of the bed lay Biscuit's old green blanket, folded into a neat square. It still smelled a little like toast and grass. Sam rubbed its soft, worn corner between his fingers. "I miss you, Biscuit," he whispered. The room did not answer, but the blanket felt warm.

Sam tried to close his eyes. He counted sheep, then stairs, then the cracks in the ceiling. Nothing helped. Every time he shut his eyes, he saw floppy ears and a wagging tail. Sam sat up. "I need to do something," he said to the dark. He just did not know what.

Mum came in, her slippers going flip-flap, flip-flap. She sat on the edge of the bed. "Can't sleep?" Sam nodded. "Biscuit always slept right there," he said, pointing at the rug. "Do you remember when he chased the leaves?" Mum asked. Sam giggled, then his eyes went wet. "He barked at them like they owed him money," Sam said, and they both laughed until the bed shook.

Then Sam had an idea. "Can we make stars? One for every good thing about Biscuit. We could hang them in the window." Mum found the crayons and a pile of yellow paper. Sam's first star came out lumpy, like a squashed potato. His second one stuck to his thumb. He wiggled his hand and made a sound like a surprised duck. "Quack!" Mum said, and Sam snorted.

He wrote on each star in wobbly letters. Biscuit liked crunchy carrots. Biscuit snored like a tractor. Biscuit waited by the gate every day for the school bus. Sam's throat felt tight, so he stopped and took a big breath before he kept going. Some stars made him smile. Some made him want to cry a little. He let both things happen.

Dad came up with a roll of tape to help hang the last star. It had a drawing of a brown dog under a big yellow sun. Sam taped it to the window beside the others. The window was open a crack, and a cool breeze slipped in. The stars turned slowly and tapped against each other with tiny papery clicks, like small paws on a wooden floor.

Sam listened. Tap, tap, tap. It was not Biscuit, but it sounded a little like him. Sam climbed back into bed and pulled the green blanket over his knees. He thought about the leaves, the snoring, and the gate. His eyelids felt heavy, as if they were made of soft wool.

The breeze grew gentle. The stars slowed down, tapping less and less. The owl called hoo, hoo, softer now. Mum turned off the lamp, and only a warm yellow glow from the hall stayed on. "Goodnight, Sam."

"Goodnight, Mum."

Sam's breathing slowed, in and out, in and out, like a dog sleeping by the fire. The last star turned once more, then stopped. The room was still and safe.

Goodnight, Biscuit.

first_draft.title: Sam and the Squeaky Trail
first_draft.text:
On a quiet evening, the kitchen smelled of warm toast, and lamplight spilled across the floorboards like honey. Sam sat at the table with his chin on his fists. At the stove, Mum hummed a soft tune, the same one she always hummed when she was thinking.

Sam's eyes drifted to the back door. There was a small brass hook there, and for as long as he could remember, Biscuit's squeaky toy had hung from it. It was a lumpy green frog with one ear chewed off. Now the hook was empty, and Sam's chest felt as heavy as a wet sponge.

Biscuit had been gone for a whole week. Sam still expected to hear his tail thumping against the cupboard door.

Sam slid off his chair and searched the kitchen. He checked under the sofa, where he found a lost crayon, a sock and a crumb-covered biscuit that was definitely not Biscuit. He lifted every cushion and peered behind the bookshelf. No frog. Each place he looked only made the empty feeling bigger.

He came back to the table and slumped down. Mum pulled the chair beside him and sat close. She didn't rush to fix anything. She just waited.

"He used to bring that frog to the door every single time I came home," Sam said. "He'd wag so hard his whole back end wiggled."

"I remember," Mum said softly. "And I'm not sure where the frog has gone, love."

Sam nodded. He stared at his toast. Then he remembered something. Every evening at dusk, Biscuit had carried that frog out through the back door, down the path, all the way to the garden gate. Sam had always followed him.

"Mum, I think I know where to look," he said. "Will you come with me?"

Mum switched on the porch light and took his hand. The grass was cool and damp under their socks. "First stop," Sam whispered, "the sunny patch."

They stood on the little square of grass where the sun always warmed the ground. "Biscuit rolled here every afternoon," Sam said. "He squished his ears flat and made the funniest snuffling noise." Mum laughed, a warm, bubbling laugh. Sam smiled, too, though his throat felt tight.

Next they tiptoed to the apple tree. "He sniffed for windfalls under here," Sam said, pointing at the roots. "He always got grass stuck in his whiskers."

At last they reached the gate. The lamp from the kitchen window glowed faintly across the yard. Sam crouched down and parted the long grass with both hands.

There, tucked in the tangle, was a lumpy green frog with one chewed ear.

Sam picked it up. It gave one soft squeak, like a tiny sigh.

"He was keeping it safe for us," Sam whispered.

Back inside, the kitchen was warm and bright. Sam carried the frog carefully, as if it might break, and reached up to the brass hook. He hung it there himself. The frog swayed gently and was still.

"Remember when he forgot to let go of it and pulled you right across the hall?" Mum asked.

Sam giggled. "He skidded on the rug and I couldn't stop laughing."

Mum wiped her eyes with her sleeve, and Sam sniffed, and they both smiled through it.

Sam wrapped himself in his blue blanket on the sofa. Mum switched off the big light and left the lamp glowing low. She hummed quietly as she cleared away the toast crumbs. The frog rested on its hook. The house grew still.

Sam's breathing slowed. Somewhere in his sleepy head, he could almost hear a soft squeak, and he smiled, and let his eyes close.

baseline.text:
In a tall oak tree, under a silver moon, lived a little owl named Maple.

Maple was very, very sleepy. Her round eyes went droop, droop, droop, like two sleepy moons. Her feathers felt as heavy as warm bread dough.

But her nest was bare. Her soft moss blanket had blown away on the evening wind.

Maple flew down to the garden. "Whoo, whoo, has anyone seen my blanket?" she called softly.

A hedgehog snuffled under a bush. "Not me," he yawned. "I have only prickles, and prickles are not cozy."

Maple fluttered on. A field mouse peeked out of the grass. "Here is a puff of dandelion fluff," she squeaked.

Maple tried it. It tickled her nose, and she sneezed. "Achoo!" It was much too thin.

Maple sighed and sat on the garden gate. The night was quiet. Then she heard a gentle hum drifting over the hill. It was the wind, rustling through the tall grass like a lullaby.

She followed the hum down the lane, past the sleepy pond, where the frogs were singing their evening songs. Her wings whispered whoosh, whoosh.

There, snagged on the old fence, was her moss blanket, soft and green and waiting. Maple tugged it free with her beak and carried it home, one slow wing beat at a time.

Back in her nest, Maple tucked the moss around her toes. She fluffed her feathers and wiggled until she was just right.

Hush, hush, sang the wind in the trees. Hush, hush, sang the leaves.

The moon climbed slowly up the sky. The wind hummed, soft as a kitten's purr. Maple's eyes drifted shut, one, two, three.

Hush, hush, goodnight, little owl. Hush, hush, goodnight, moon. Hush, hush, goodnight, tree.
