first_draft.title: Hazel and the Lantern Hollow
first_draft.text:
Hazel was a small, sleepy owl with soft gray feathers. She sat in her nest at the top of the old oak tree, blinking slowly. Blink. Blink. But the leaves went rustle, rustle, rustle, and the moon was cold and bright. Hazel could not settle. She shuffled left. She shuffled right. "Hoo, hoo," she sighed. "I am too sleepy to sleep."

Then a stream whispered far below. Shh, shh, shh. Hazel tilted her head. "Maybe a little walk will help," she said. So she spread her wings and drifted out into the quiet woods.

Silver moss glowed under her feet. Hazel drifted past it, slow and light. Plip, plop, went the stream as it wandered between the trees. A sleepy frog sat on a stone with its eyes half shut. "Ribbit," it said softly. Hazel blinked back at it.

Next, a hedgehog gave a big round yawn, and Hazel yawned too. She found a fallen log and settled on top. Bump. Lump. Bump. "Too lumpy," she murmured, and she hopped off again.

Then, between the trees, a golden glow flickered. One lantern. Two. Three. They swayed like friendly fireflies, and Hazel followed them along the bank of the stream, past the silver moss, to a great hollow tree.

A gentle badger stood in the doorway, holding up a lantern. "Come in, little owl," rumbled Old Mossy, in his warm, deep voice. "We keep a light burning for lost night creatures. Are you lost?" "Not lost," said Hazel. "Only too sleepy to settle."

Old Mossy nodded. "Then try my hum." Hazel began to hum, soft and low, like wind in a quilt. Mmmmm. Mmmmm. The frog hummed. The hedgehog hummed. Old Mossy rumbled along, and the whole hollow hummed together.

Hazel curled into a cozy corner beside the warm lantern. Her feathers puffed up like a pillow. Her blinks grew slower and slower.

The creatures murmured and yawned. The lanterns dimmed to small golden glows. Outside, the stream hummed its slow song. Hazel's blinks grew longer, and longer, until her eyes closed. Hmmm, she breathed. The forest went quiet and still.

request: A girl who explores a mysterious cave and finds something amazing

baseline.title: Zoe and the Glowing Cave
baseline.text:
On a breezy Saturday, Zoe climbed the green hill behind Grandpa Joe's house. Her tortoise, Pebble, rode in a soft backpack with his wrinkly head poking out to sniff the wind. Pebble was very slow, but Zoe did not mind. Slow was good for looking.

At the top of the hill, a dark mouth opened in the rock. Cool air breathed out, smelling of wet stone and rain. "A cave!" Zoe whispered. Her heart went thump, thump, thump.

"Stay close, Zoe-bird," said Grandpa, clicking on his flashlight. "We explore together, one careful step at a time."

Zoe clicked on her own flashlight, and they stepped inside. Drip. Plink. Plop. Somewhere far away, water sang a tinkly tune. The walls were bumpy and gray, like the back of a sleepy elephant. Then the tunnel curved, and Zoe gasped.

Crystals! They grew from the walls and ceiling in clusters, pale pink and deep purple and clear as ice. When her flashlight touched them, they sparkled like a hundred tiny stars. Some glowed softly from inside, as if someone had hidden lanterns in the rock.

"Grandpa, look at them all," Zoe breathed. "It's like the inside of a jewel box."

Then came a sound: scritch, scratch, scrape.

Zoe spun around. Pebble had wriggled out of the backpack and was crawling across the floor toward a narrow crack. Before Zoe could call out, his shell slid into the gap and stuck fast between two rocks.

"Pebble!" Zoe cried. She dropped to her knees. Pebble pulled forward. He pushed back. He did not move at all. He let out a little huff, and his tiny legs paddled the air.

"Oh, Pebble, don't be scared," Zoe said, her voice wobbling. "I'm here."

Grandpa knelt beside her. "Let's think, Zoe. What do we know?"

"Pebble is stuck," said Zoe. "And the rock won't let go."

She gripped Pebble's shell and tugged gently. Nothing. Grandpa tried lifting the top rock with both hands. It did not budge. "That one's too heavy for us," he said. "We need a cleverer plan."

Zoe shut her eyes and took a slow breath, the way Mama did when the wind made her nervous. Then she opened her eyes and shone her flashlight into the crack. Beneath Pebble's shell, a thin, flat stone was tucked under the big one, like a wedge under a door. If they could tip that thin stone out, the big rock might loosen.

"Grandpa, your walking stick!" Zoe said. "Could it be a lever?"

Grandpa grinned. "Brilliant idea, Zoe-bird."

He slid the end of the stick under the thin stone. Zoe held her breath. Grandpa pushed slowly, slowly. The stone tipped, and with a little rumble, the big rock shifted just enough. Zoe slid her hands under Pebble and wiggled him left, then right, then left again.

Pop! Pebble tumbled free onto a soft patch of dust. He blinked, then slowly tucked his head back into his shell, as if to say, "That was a lot of work."

Zoe laughed so hard her flashlight wobbled. "You're safe, Pebble! You're safe!"

Pebble had a tiny scratch on his shell. Grandpa said it would heal like a scrape on a knee. Zoe checked him twice to be sure.

Then she looked back at the crystals, glowing in the dim light. "Grandpa, can I take one home? Just a little one? My collection would be the best ever."

Grandpa sat down on a flat rock and patted the space beside him. "These crystals grew for thousands of years, Zoe. Each one took a very long time, drop by drop. If we take one, the cave loses something, and so does everyone who comes after us."

Zoe thought about it. She looked at the pink clusters and the purple points and the lantern glow. She looked at Pebble, who was happily munching a leaf he had found in the bottom of the backpack.

"Maybe I can draw them instead," she said slowly. "Then I can show my friends, and nobody's crystal goes missing."

"That's a wonderful idea," Grandpa said, and his eyes were warm. "The best treasures are the ones we share, and the ones we leave whole for the next explorer to find."

Zoe took out her notebook and colored pencils. She drew the pink clusters, the purple points, and the glow inside the stone. Pebble poked his head out to watch, and Grandpa held the flashlight steady.

When they walked back down the hill, the sun was warm and gold. Zoe carried Pebble in her backpack and the notebook in her hands, and she felt happy all the way down.

That night, Zoe lay in bed with her blanket pulled up to her chin. Her nightlight made a soft circle on the ceiling. Pebble rested in his box by the window. Zoe ran her finger over her drawing and remembered the gentle drip of the cave, a tinkling sound, far away and quiet.

Her eyes grew heavy.

"Goodnight, crystals," she whispered. "Goodnight, Pebble."

Pebble's shell gave a tiny click, and the room was still.

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Humming Crystal
first_draft.text:
The meadow was turning the color of toast when Zoe tiptoed through the gate, a flashlight in one hand and Pebble tucked under her other arm. Pebble was a slow tortoise, but he was never late for an adventure, and tonight he had brought his own kind of light: two bright, round eyes that noticed everything.

"Ready?" whispered Zoe.

Pebble blinked once. That meant yes. He blinked twice when he saw something worth a second look.

They crossed the sleepy meadow, past clover heads folded up for the night, to a dark hole in a grey hill. Cool air breathed out of it, smelling of rain and wet stone. Pebble stopped and peered at a thin crack beside the entrance, where a little draft whistled through. He blinked twice, then tucked the thought away for later.

"Hello?" called Zoe. "Is anybody in there?"

A soft light blinked on deep inside, then another, then a whole line of them, like lanterns being lit one by one. Out bobbed Figgy the glowworm, glowing the color of warm honey.

"Visitors! Lovely, lovely visitors!" Figgy hummed a happy tune that wandered off key twice before it reached the end. "Mind the step. Mind the second step. Mind the third step, which is the wobbly one. I am Figgy, the finest light in the whole cave, and I light every passage, every corner and every crack. Follow me!"

Zoe checked the ceiling, then the floor, then the ceiling again. She always checked every corner twice. "Are there sleepy creatures in here?"

"Oh, dozens!" said Figgy. "Hedgehogs in the dry nooks, moles in the soft pools, and a family of frogs who are only grumpy before breakfast."

They walked on, deeper and deeper, until the tunnel opened into a round room. Crystals grew from the walls like frosted icicles, pink and blue and pale violet, and in the middle stood one enormous crystal that glowed like a sleepy moon.

It was humming. Zoe pressed her ear against its cool side and heard a lullaby, rising and falling like a rocking boat. Then the tune broke off in the middle, with a small sad click, like a music box that had run out of winding.

From the nooks, prickly heads poked out. Hedgehogs yawned. Moles blinked up from the pools with their paws over their mouths. "It's been stuck like that since teatime," sniffed one mole. "We can't settle until the song is whole again."

"Then we'll find the missing notes," said Zoe, and she squared her shoulders. "Which way?"

Figgy zoomed toward a long, echoing tunnel. "This way! This way! Hold on to your hats!"

Zoe cupped her hands around her mouth and shouted, "Hello!"

"Hello... lo... lo..." the tunnel called back. But something was missing. The last note came back as a whisper of a whisper, as if it had tripped on the way.

"Let me help!" Figgy puffed up his glow and hummed loudly. His tune was so wobbly that the echo came back as a squeaky gate. "Oops," said Figgy. "Perhaps I am a little loud."
